page: Vultr voc-m-1c-8gb-50s-amd is an x86_64 architecture virtual server within the Optimized Cloud Compute family. It is configured with a single shared AMD EPYC vCPU running at 2.0 GHz, consisting of one physical core and one thread. The system is equipped with 8.0 GB of RAM, establishing a high 1:8 vCPU-to-memory ratio. Local storage is provided via a bundled 50 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No GPU hardware is present on this instance type.

Benchmark data indicates a significant divergence between single-core processing capabilities and memory subsystem throughput. The single-core stress-ng CPU test registers at 2896.39, placing the processor in the top 25% tier. Conversely, multi-core performance is limited by the single-vCPU allocation, scoring in the bottom 25%. Memory bandwidth is a primary bottleneck, with read-only small block cached bandwidth at 130.9 GB/sec and large block uncached bandwidth at 22.42 GB/sec, both falling into the bottom 10% of tested hardware. Passmark database operations and Redis SET operations also rank in the bottom 10%, reflecting the constraints of the shared CPU and memory architecture.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, this server offers a high memory allocation relative to its single shared vCPU, making it a resource-dense option for memory-bound workloads that do not require continuous, dedicated CPU performance. The primary tradeoff is the shared CPU allocation and constrained memory bandwidth, which limits its utility for high-throughput database operations or intensive multi-threaded processing.

This server configuration is suitable for lightweight, memory-intensive applications, small-scale single-threaded web serving, basic text processing, and low-concurrency development environments. It is less suited for high-traffic databases, parallel computing, or large-scale LLM inference.

This 1:8 vCPU-to-memory ratio is paired with a bundled 50 GB NVMe SSD. Benchmark results show strong single-core CPU performance in stress-ng tests, but multi-core and memory bandwidth metrics fall into the lower percentiles, with uncached read bandwidth at 22.42 GB/sec. Database and Redis operations also show lower-tier performance due to the shared CPU and memory bottlenecks. Qualitatively, this instance provides a cost-effective entry point for memory-heavy, low-CPU workloads. It is best suited for lightweight web serving, single-threaded applications, and development environments requiring more memory than typical entry-level instances.
